title: Coasts 2: Coastal Landforms
subject: Geography
description: Headlands and bays, concordant and discordant coasts, the eroding headland, wave-cut platforms, spits, bars, tombolos and sand dunes.
author: Erick

cards.front: Headland
cards.back: An area of land that sticks out from the coast (usually hard rock).

cards.front: Bay
cards.back: A curve inland along the coast (usually soft rock).

cards.front: Differential erosion
cards.back: When hard rock and soft rock are next to each other, perpendicular to the sea, and erode at different rates.

cards.front: Examples of hard (resistant) rock
cards.back: Limestone / chalk

cards.front: Examples of soft (less resistant) rock
cards.back: Mudstone / sandstone / clay

cards.front: Explain how headlands and bays are formed.
cards.back: They form because of differences in geology. Soft rock erodes faster and forms bays. Hard rock erodes more slowly and is left sticking out as headlands.
cards.imageAlt: Plan view of hard rock headlands either side of a soft rock bay

cards.front: Discordant coastline
cards.back: Bands of hard and soft rock run perpendicular (at right angles) to the coast, so headlands and bays form.

cards.front: Concordant coastline
cards.back: Bands of rock run parallel to the coast. The hard rock protects the soft rock behind it. If the sea breaks through, it can erode a cove (e.g. Lulworth Cove).

cards.front: Swanage, Dorset: which rocks form the headlands?
cards.back: Limestone and chalk (hard rock)

cards.front: Swanage, Dorset: which rock forms the bays?
cards.back: Clay (soft rock)

cards.front: Put the eroding headland sequence in order.
cards.back: Crack → cave → arch → large arch → stack → stump → wave-cut platform

cards.front: Eroding headland: how does a cave form?
cards.back: Marine erosion weakens the headland along lines of weakness and cracks start to form. The crack grows into a cave.

cards.front: Eroding headland: how does an arch form?
cards.back: The cave is eroded until it breaks through to the other side of the headland.

cards.front: Eroding headland: how does a stack form?
cards.back: The arch gets bigger as the material above is weakened, until the roof collapses, leaving a stack (a pillar of rock).

cards.front: Eroding headland: how does a stump form?
cards.back: The stack is eroded down over time into a stump. Finally it becomes a wave-cut platform at sea level.

cards.front: Eroding headland: name the feature labelled A.
cards.back: Crack

cards.front: Explain the formation of a wave-cut notch.
cards.back: Waves erode the base of a cliff between high and low tide (by hydraulic action and abrasion), cutting a notch.
cards.imageAlt: Cliff with a wave-cut notch at high tide level and a wave-cut platform

cards.front: Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform.
cards.back: The notch gets deeper until the cliff above collapses. This repeats, so the cliff retreats and leaves a flat rocky platform that is exposed at low tide.
cards.imageAlt: Cliff with a wave-cut notch at high tide level and a wave-cut platform

cards.front: Explain the formation of a spit.
cards.back: Longshore drift carries material along the coast. Where the coast changes direction, material is deposited out into the sea, forming a long ridge of sand or shingle. Changing winds can curve the end (recurved end) and salt marsh forms behind it.
cards.imageAlt: Plan view of a spit growing out from a bend in the coast

cards.front: Bar
cards.back: A spit that grows right across a bay, joining two headlands and trapping a lagoon behind it.

cards.front: Tombolo
cards.back: A spit or bar that joins the mainland to an island.

cards.front: Sand dunes: what begins the process?
cards.back: An obstacle on the beach. Sand is deposited around it, making it larger.

cards.front: Embryo dune
cards.back: Forms as more and more sand is deposited around an obstacle.

cards.front: Fore dune
cards.back: Forms when embryo dunes build up and join together.

cards.front: Yellow dune
cards.back: Mobile and often the largest dune.

cards.front: Grey dune
cards.back: Plants die and decay forming humus (soil); the dead plant material turns the sand grey. With more soil and vegetation the dune becomes fixed.

cards.front: Mature dune
cards.back: Once the dunes are fixed, trees begin to grow. Diversity decreases because trees take most of the water, sunlight and nutrients.

cards.front: Dune slack
cards.back: A damp hollow between dunes where the water table reaches the surface.

cards.front: What role does marram grass play in sand dunes?
cards.back: It colonises the dune, resists drought, grows upwards as it is buried, and its roots anchor the sand and prevent erosion.

cards.front: Why are early dunes alkaline?
cards.back: Because of calcareous (calcium-rich) sea shells in the sand.

cards.front: Why are later dunes more acidic?
cards.back: The calcium is washed away by rainwater.

cards.front: Why do only salt-tolerant plants grow near the sea?
cards.back: Early dunes are salty and have extremely good drainage, so conditions are harsh.

cards.front: How does soil change the drainage of a dune?
cards.back: The soil slows down the drainage of water, so a greater variety of plants can grow.

cards.front: Why do foredunes move inland?
cards.back: Sand builds up on the leeward (sheltered) side, where conditions are less harsh.

questions.question: Why do bays form?
options: Soft rock erodes faster than hard rock
questions.explanation: Soft rock such as clay erodes faster than hard rock, forming bays between headlands.

questions.question: What comes straight after a cave in the eroding headland sequence?
questions.explanation: Crack → cave → arch → stack → stump → wave-cut platform.

questions.question: Which is an example of soft rock?
questions.explanation: Clay, mudstone and sandstone are soft. Limestone and chalk are hard.

questions.question: Which dune is mobile and often the largest?
questions.explanation: The yellow dune is mobile and often the largest.

questions.question: What does marram grass do?
options: Anchors the sand with its roots
questions.explanation: Marram grass roots anchor the sand and prevent erosion.

questions.question: A landform that joins the mainland to an island is a...
questions.explanation: A tombolo joins an island to the mainland. A bar joins two headlands.
